190.title: Al-Layl: the giver
190.hook: the one who gives and guards himself, We ease him toward ease (92:5–7)
190.tomorrow: Ash-Shams: the sun and her brightness
190.howItsDone: Many Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, quietly and without being asked, alongside the obligatory zakat; the closing verses of Al-Layl are often recalled as the picture of giving for God's sake alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Layl, the night, and the line that says your strivings go in different directions. Your line was efforts differ. Where did your effort actually go? Day one hundred ninety.

You probably know someone who makes giving look effortless. They pick up the bill before you've noticed it arrived. They drop off soup when you're sick without asking whether you want soup. And you probably know the opposite feeling from the inside: the tight little hesitation before you hand something over, the math running in your head. What's odd is that the generous person rarely seems poorer for it. They seem lighter. Yesterday Al-Layl said our efforts go in different directions. Today it names the two directions, and it makes a claim about which one gets easier with time. Today: the giver.
screen: `THE ONE WHO PICKS UP THE BILL.` → `THE TIGHT LITTLE HESITATION.` → `TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Right after the oaths, the surah draws two portraits. The first, in verses five to seven: the one who gives, who is mindful of God, and who affirms what is good. Then, in Pickthall's words: Surely We will ease his way unto the state of ease. The second portrait, verses eight to ten, is the mirror: the one who holds back, who thinks he needs no one, and who denies the good. For him, the way is eased toward hardship. Listen to the words for ease and hardship: al-yusra and al-'usra. They're the same pair we met a few days ago in Ash-Sharh, with hardship comes ease. Here they become directions of travel. Commentators notice something striking in the grammar. Both people are eased. The road smooths out for each of them, just toward different places. Giving makes giving easier; holding back makes holding back easier. Anyone who's tried to build or break a habit knows the feeling. Then the surah returns to the giver, near its end. Verses seventeen to twenty-one describe the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay a favor anyone did him, seeking only the face of his Lord, the Most High. And the last line of the surah is a promise: he will be content. Many commentators say these closing verses were revealed about Abu Bakr, who spent his money buying the freedom of enslaved believers, Bilal among them. That's a report in the tafsir, not in the text. The text leaves the giver unnamed, so anyone can fit.
screen: `TWO PORTRAITS: GIVE, OR HOLD BACK.` · `YUSRA AND 'USRA — EASE AND HARDSHIP.` · `BOTH ROADS GET EASIER.` · `GIVING WITH NOTHING OWED.` · then, large: `GIVING MAKES IT EASY.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, sit and think of the people around you this week. Let one come to mind who could use something, and hasn't asked. A message, a meal, a ride, some time. Picture giving it before they ask. Notice where the hesitation shows up in your body, if it does. Then decide what you'll give, and when. The bell holds the time.
Al-Layl. The night, Surah ninety-two: the giver is eased toward ease, and the one who holds back toward hardship. Today's word.
Your line: giving makes it easy. Give one thing today that nobody asked you for, and notice whether the next time is a little easier. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Ash-Shams: the sun and her brightness
191.hook: eleven oaths by sun, moon, day, night, sky and earth (91:1–7)
191.howItsDone: Ash-Shams is one of the short surahs often recited in the prayer, especially the evening and night prayers; many Muslims learn its run of oaths by heart as children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Layl and the giver, eased toward ease. Your line was giving makes it easy. Did you give one thing nobody asked for? Day one hundred ninety-one.

When did you last watch the sun actually go down? Not glance at it through a windshield. Watch it, the whole slow slide, the way the light goes orange and then pink and then the sky goes on glowing after the sun itself is gone. Most of us see about a hundred sunsets a year and look at maybe two. The surah before Al-Layl in the Qur'an won't let you skip it. It opens with a string of oaths, one after another, and every one points at something you walk under every day and mostly ignore. Today: Ash-Shams, the sun.
screen: `A HUNDRED SUNSETS A YEAR.` → `WE LOOK AT MAYBE TWO.` → `ASH-SHAMS, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-one begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the sun and his brightness. In Arabic the sun, shams, is grammatically feminine, which is why our title says her brightness; Pickthall's English says his. And the word for brightness, duha, is one you know: it's the name of the morning surah from a few days ago, the full light of mid-morning. Then the oaths keep coming. By the moon when it follows the sun. By the day when it shows the sun's glory. By the night when it covers it. By the sky and the One who built it. By the earth and the One who spread it out. By the soul and the One who shaped it. Commentators count eleven things sworn by, more than in any other surah. Why swear at all? In Arabic, an oath is a way of saying: stop, look at this, what comes next matters. The things sworn by are witnesses. And look at the order. It starts huge and far away, the sun, and moves steadily closer: moon, day and night, sky, earth, and then, last, the soul. The whole universe, and then you. It's like a camera zooming from space down to a single face. Where the zoom lands is tomorrow's lesson. Today is the zoom itself: the idea that the ordinary sky is worth an oath. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told a companion who was making the night prayer too long for the people behind him to recite shorter surahs, and a hadith in Muslim's collection names Ash-Shams among them. Short enough for a tired crowd, big enough to hold the whole sky.

segments.voice: Wherever you are, find the light. A window, a patch of sun on the floor, the glow of the sky. For two minutes, just look at it. Notice its color, where it falls, how it changes things. If it's night, picture the last sunset you remember, as clearly as you can. And tonight or tomorrow, if you can, watch the sun rise or set, all of it. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Shams. The sun, the name of Surah ninety-one, which opens with eleven oaths, from the sun down to the soul. Today's word.
Your line: by the sun. When you step outside today, stop for three seconds and look at the light as if it were worth an oath. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: Ash-Shams: the soul
192.hook: by the soul and its shaping, successful is the one who purifies it (91:7–10)
192.carry: the one who purifies it succeeds
192.howItsDone: Muslims speak of tazkiyah, the lifelong work of purifying the soul, through prayer, remembrance, charity and watching one's habits; the verse on success in Ash-Shams is one of the texts most often quoted about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Shams, and a run of oaths from the sun down through the sky and the earth. Your line was by the sun. Did you stop and look at the light? Day one hundred ninety-two.

Yesterday the camera zoomed. It started with the sun, moved past the moon, the day and night, the sky, the earth, and then it stopped on something small enough to fit inside you. Here's where the eleven oaths were heading all along. Not a star, not a mountain. A soul. Yours, and everyone's. And after all that buildup, the surah says one thing about the soul, one sentence about what success actually is. It isn't what most of us would put on a list of successful people. Today: the soul.
screen: `THE CAMERA STOPS.` → `NOT A STAR. A SOUL.` → `WHAT SUCCESS ACTUALLY IS.`

segments.voice: Verse seven: by the soul, nafs, and the One who shaped it and made it well-proportioned. Verse eight: and inspired it with its wickedness and its mindfulness. Both, in the same soul, from the start. The surah doesn't pretend people are pure by default, or rotten by default. It says the soul knows both roads. Then the sentence all eleven oaths were building to. In Pickthall's words: He is indeed successful who causeth it to grow. And the next verse, the mirror: the one who buries it, who stunts it, has failed. The Arabic verb for the first is zakkaha. You've heard the root: zakat, the giving that is one of the five pillars. Z-k-y carries two ideas at once, to purify and to grow, the way pruning a plant cleans it and makes it grow stronger. So zakat purifies wealth, and this verse says a person can do the same to a soul. The opposite verb, dassaha, means to bury something, to hide it in the dirt. Scholars call the work of the first verb tazkiyah, purification of the soul, and whole books have been written about it. But the verse itself is plain. Success isn't money or followers here. It's what you did with the soul you were given: did you tend it, or bury it? The surah then ends with a short, sharp story, the people of Thamud who hamstrung the she-camel they'd been warned to leave alone. An example of a soul buried, a whole people at a time.
screen: `THE SOUL KNOWS BOTH ROADS.` · `ZAKKAHA — TO PURIFY AND TO GROW.` · `DASSAHA — TO BURY IT IN THE DIRT.` · `SUCCESS: WHAT YOU DID WITH IT.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO PURIFIES IT SUCCEEDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and for two minutes think of one small habit that clouds your day a little. The scroll before sleep. The sharp reply. The thing you say about a coworker. Just one, and small. Picture pruning it: one cut, not a whole new life. Decide what the cut looks like today. If you pray, you can ask for help with it in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Shams. The sun, Surah ninety-one, whose eleven oaths end on the soul: successful is the one who purifies it. Today's word.
Your line: the one who purifies it succeeds. Make the one small cut you chose, once, today. Tending is done in small cuts. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: Al-Balad: the steep path
193.hook: he has not attempted the steep path: freeing a slave, feeding in hunger (90:11–16)
193.tomorrow: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
193.howItsDone: Many Muslims give food to the hungry as sadaqah, especially to poor relatives and orphans, and support charities that pay off debts or free people from bondage, reading these verses of Al-Balad as a description of the harder road.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Shams, and the soul that can be tended or buried. Your line was the one who purifies it succeeds. Did you make your one small cut? Day one hundred ninety-three.
screen: `ASH-SHAMS — THE ONE WHO PURIFIES IT SUCCEEDS.`

segments.voice: Anyone who has hiked a mountain knows the moment the trail forks. One way is the switchback path, long and gentle, crowded with people in sneakers. The other goes straight up, rocks and roots, and your legs are already complaining at the thought. Most of us, most days, take the gentle one. The surah before Ash-Shams uses exactly this picture, a hard mountain road, and then asks a question that sounds like a riddle: do you know what the steep path is? The answer isn't a mountain at all. Today: Al-Balad, the city, and the steep path.
screen: `THE TRAIL FORKS.` → `GENTLE, OR STRAIGHT UP?` → `WHAT IS THE STEEP PATH?`

segments.voice: Surah ninety opens with an oath by this city, al-balad, which commentators take to be Mecca, the Prophet's own city, where he and his followers were being made unwelcome. Then it describes a certain kind of person, loud about the money he's spent, sure nobody sees him. And then verse eleven, in Pickthall's words: But he hath not attempted the Ascent. The Arabic is al-'aqabah, a steep mountain pass, the kind of road that makes you lean forward and use your hands. And then the riddle. What will tell you what the steep path is? Here is the answer, verses thirteen to sixteen. Freeing a neck, meaning freeing someone who is enslaved. Feeding, on a day of hunger, an orphan who is a relative, or a poor person lying in the dust. That's it. That's the mountain. Not a spiritual feat, not a vision. Setting someone free, and feeding someone hungry. Why is that steep? Because it costs. The man at the start of the surah spent plenty, and bragged about it. The steep path is spending where nobody claps: on a relative you're a little tired of helping, on a stranger in the dust. Verse seventeen adds one more step: to be among those who believe and who urge each other to patience and to compassion. So the climb isn't done alone. People on the steep path pull each other up. In the Prophet's time, freeing enslaved people was a real and costly act, and the Qur'an returns to it again and again. Today, many Muslims read this verse as a call to free people from every kind of bondage, including debt.

segments.voice: Sit for two minutes, and think about food today. Who near you might be hungry, or just tired of cooking for themselves? A neighbor, a relative, a coworker who skips lunch, someone you pass on the street. Choose one person, and one way to feed them today: a meal, a coffee, a donation to a food bank. Hold the choice until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Al-Balad. The city, Surah ninety, which names the steep path: freeing someone, and feeding the hungry. Today's word.
Your line: take the steep path. Feed one person today, especially someone it costs you a little to feed. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
194.hook: have We not given him two eyes, a tongue and lips, and shown him two ways (90:8–10)
194.tomorrow: Al-Fajr: the dawn and ten nights
194.howItsDone: Muslims often recall these verses of Al-Balad when speaking of guarding the tongue, a theme that runs through many hadith, and of gratitude for the senses as gifts that come with responsibility.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Balad, the city, and the climb it names: freeing someone, feeding the hungry. Your line was take the steep path. Did you feed someone? Day one hundred ninety-four.

Try this. Touch your eyelids, gently. Then your lips. Then press your tongue against the back of your teeth. You've used all three thousands of times today without a thought. Reading this screen. Talking to the barista. Tasting your coffee. Muttering at the traffic. They're the most ordinary equipment a person owns. Right before the steep path we climbed yesterday, Al-Balad stops and points at exactly this equipment, and asks a question about it. Then it adds one more gift that you can't touch at all. Today: two eyes, a tongue, two lips.
screen: `TOUCH YOUR EYELIDS. YOUR LIPS.` → `THE MOST ORDINARY EQUIPMENT.` → `ONE GIFT YOU CAN'T TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Al-Balad describes a man who boasts that he has spent heaps of money and thinks no one sees him. The surah answers with a question, verse eight, in Pickthall's words: Did We not assign unto him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips? The man who thinks no one sees him was given the power to see. The man bragging with his mouth was given the mouth. It's a gentle, almost funny reversal. Everything he's using to show off was handed to him. Why two lips, and not just a mouth? Commentators notice that lips close. The tongue can speak, and the lips can hold it back. The same equipment can say the cruel thing or keep it in. Then verse ten: and We showed him the two ways. The Arabic is an-najdayn, the two raised roads, the two highland paths. Most commentators read it as the way of good and the way of harm, both shown clearly, like two roads on a ridge you can see from far off. A minority, reported by Ibn Kathir, read it more tenderly, as the two sources of milk a newborn is guided to without being taught. Either way, the point is the same: guidance was given before you asked for it. Eyes to see the roads. A tongue to speak on the good one. Lips to stop at the other. And then, verse eleven, which we read yesterday: but he did not attempt the steep path. So the surah's logic runs: you were given the tools, you were shown the roads, now climb.

segments.voice: Sit for two minutes and rest your attention on your mouth. Feel the tongue resting, the lips closed. Then think of one thing you could say today that would help someone: a thank you, an apology, a word of praise to someone who never hears it. Let the lips stay closed for now. Just choose the words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Balad. The city, Surah ninety: eyes, a tongue, two lips, and the two roads shown. Today's word.
Your line: two roads shown. Use your tongue once today for good, and once, let your lips close on something that didn't need saying. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: Al-Fajr: the dawn and ten nights
195.hook: by the dawn and ten nights, taken as the first ten of Dhul Hijjah (89:1–2)
195.howItsDone: Muslims pray fajr, the dawn prayer, in the first light before sunrise; in the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah many fast, give charity and say the takbir often, taking these as the ten nights of Surah 89.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Balad, and the eyes, tongue and lips we were given, and the two roads shown. Your line was two roads shown. Did you use your tongue once for good? Day one hundred ninety-five.

There's a particular kind of quiet at five in the morning. The streetlights are still on. The birds start before the traffic does. If you've ever had a newborn, or an early shift, or a flight to catch, you've met it. Most people only know that hour by accident. But in a Muslim household, it's the start of the day on purpose: the first of the five prayers is called by the name of that hour, before the sun comes up. And the surah just before Al-Balad in the Qur'an opens by swearing by it. Today: Al-Fajr, the dawn.
screen: `FIVE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE BIRDS BEFORE THE TRAFFIC.` → `AL-FAJR, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-nine opens, in Pickthall's words: By the Dawn And ten nights. Fajr comes from a root that means to break open, to burst through, the way water bursts out of the ground as a spring. Dawn is the moment light breaks through the dark. It's also the name of the first daily prayer, prayed in the gray light before sunrise, when many people are still asleep. And ten nights. Which ten? The surah doesn't say. Most commentators say they are the first ten nights of Dhul Hijjah, the month of the Hajj, the days leading up to the pilgrimage's high point and the feast of Eid al-Adha. Others say the last ten nights of Ramadan, and some say the first ten of Muharram. The text leaves the question open, and scholars have held it open respectfully for centuries. For the Dhul Hijjah reading, many point to a hadith in Bukhari: there are no days in which good deeds are dearer to God than these ten days. So in those days, many Muslims fast, give more, and repeat Allahu akbar often, even if they're nowhere near Mecca. Then the surah keeps swearing: by the even and the odd, by the night as it moves on. And it asks, is there not in this an oath for someone with sense? The word for sense, hijr, means something that holds you back, a check, like a wall. The oaths are for the person whose mind can stop and notice. So: a dawn, some nights, a question. The first stop in a surah we'll walk through for four days.
screen: `FAJR — LIGHT BREAKING THROUGH.` · `THE FIRST PRAYER OF THE DAY.` · `TEN NIGHTS: WHICH TEN?` · `AN OATH FOR SOMEONE WITH SENSE.` · then, large: `BY THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, picture the earliest dawn you can remember seeing. The gray, the first bird, the cool air. Stay there. Then make a small plan: pick one morning this week to wake before sunrise, even by ten minutes, and just watch the light arrive. If you pray, that's the time of fajr. If you don't, it's still worth seeing. The bell holds the time.
Al-Fajr. The dawn, the light breaking through, the first prayer of the day and the name of Surah eighty-nine. Today's word.
Your line: by the dawn. Set an alarm tonight for one early morning this week, and give the first light your full attention. Day one hundred ninety-five.

fork.reveal: most say the nights leading up to the Hajj and Eid al-Adha. others say the last ten of Ramadan or the first ten of Muharram.

original.note: Arabic: the dawn, from f-j-r, to burst open, as a spring bursts from the ground.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about early mornings.
what it means: oaths by the dawn, ten sacred nights, the even and odd, and the passing night, for anyone with sense to notice.
what a scholar hears: f-j-r also gives tafjir, making water gush (17:90–91); the ten nights are unspecified in the text, and the Dhul Hijjah reading leans on Bukhari's hadith on the ten days.

196.title: Al-Fajr: the old cities
196.hook: 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh built high and went too far (89:6–13)
196.howItsDone: Muslims read the Qur'an's accounts of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh as lessons about pride and power; many who visit ancient ruins recall these verses and reflect on the peoples who built them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fajr, the dawn, and ten nights nobody can quite pin down. Your line was by the dawn. Did you set that alarm? Day one hundred ninety-six.

Every big city has one. The tower built to be the tallest, the name on the side in letters you can read from the highway. And every traveler has stood somewhere else, among broken columns in a desert or a jungle, reading a sign that says a great city stood here, and wondering what the people thought when they built it. Did they think it would last? The second passage of Al-Fajr takes the listener on exactly that kind of tour, through three peoples who built high. Today: the old cities.
screen: `THE TOWER WITH ITS NAME ON THE SIDE.` → `BROKEN COLUMNS IN THE DESERT.` → `THE OLD CITIES.`

segments.voice: Verse six asks: have you not seen what your Lord did with 'Ad? Then three stops. First, 'Ad, and Iram, the city of pillars, whose like was never made in any land. 'Ad were an ancient Arabian people; their prophet, the Qur'an says elsewhere, was Hud. People have searched for Iram for centuries, and nobody knows for certain where it stood. Second, Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley. Their prophet was Salih. Muslims have long connected them with al-Hijr in northwest Arabia, where huge facades are cut into sandstone; archaeologists date those carvings to the Nabataeans, a later people, so the link is tradition, not settled history. Third, Pharaoh, lord of the stakes. Commentators read the stakes as the pegs of great tents or armies, or as monuments fixed firmly in the ground, or as a way he punished people. All three, verse eleven says, overstepped in the land and multiplied corruption. And then, in Pickthall's words: Lo! thy Lord is ever watchful. The Arabic is bil-mirsad, on the lookout, like a watchtower on a road. Notice the irony. These were builders of pillars and towers and monuments, and the surah says the real watchtower was never theirs. The Qur'an isn't against building. It's against building as a way of saying I don't answer to anyone. It's the end of a week. We began with Al-Layl, the giver eased toward ease, then the sun, and the soul that can be tended or buried. Then the steep path and the two roads. Then the dawn. Today, the towers.
screen: `'AD AND IRAM, THE CITY OF PILLARS.` · `THAMUD, WHO CARVED THE ROCK.` · `PHARAOH, LORD OF THE STAKES.` · `YOUR LORD IS ON THE WATCHTOWER.` · then, large: `TOWERS FALL.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, think of something built to impress. A skyscraper, a stadium, a mansion online, or something of your own: a resume, a profile, a car. Picture it a thousand years from now: sand, grass, a sign for tourists. Don't be gloomy about it. Just notice what would still matter about the people who lived there. The bell holds the time.
Al-Fajr. The dawn, Surah eighty-nine, which walks past 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, and says your Lord is ever watchful. Today's word.
Your line: towers fall. The next time you pass something built to impress, ask what will outlast it. Day one hundred ninety-six.

myth: archaeologists have found and confirmed the site of Iram
people have searched for centuries; nobody knows for certain where it stood.
the rock facades at al-Hijr are dated by archaeologists to the Nabataeans
the link to Thamud is a long tradition, not settled history.
Al-Fajr condemns building itself
it condemns overstepping and corruption: building as a way of answering to no one.

fork.setup: three peoples built high and overstepped. what does Al-Fajr say right after their stories?
options: their cities will be rebuilt
your Lord is ever watchful
no one remembers them
fork.reveal: Lo! thy Lord is ever watchful (89:14): on the watchtower, bil-mirsad. the builders of towers were never the ones watching.

original.note: Arabic: "Iram of the pillars," the city of 'Ad (Qur'an 89:7); its location is unknown.

trapdoor: what you thought: old stories about cities that were destroyed.
what it means: three peoples who built high and overstepped, and the reminder that the Lord is on the watch.

what a scholar hears: dhu al-awtad, lord of the stakes, has at least three readings in tafsir; al-Hijr's facades are Nabataean, first century BCE to CE, while Thamud is attested in older Assyrian records.
